title: What Does Contract Cleaners Insurance Cover? A Section Guide
excerpt: A plain-English, section-by-section breakdown of what contract cleaners insurance covers, what it usually excludes, and the limits contract clients expect to see.
metaDescription: A section-by-section guide to what contract cleaners insurance cover includes, from public and employers' liability to keys, equipment and treatment risk.
keywords: what does contract cleaners insurance cover
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Two cleaners in uniform working in an office corridor with a mop bucket and wet floor sign
content:
Contract cleaners insurance is not one single product. It is a package of separate sections sitting inside one policy, each one covering a different type of loss: injury to other people, injury to your own staff, damage to a client's building or contents, the keys you hold, the machinery in your van, and the advice or specifications you give as a cleaning contractor. When a client asks for "proof of insurance" before signing a cleaning contract, they are usually asking about two or three of those sections in particular.

In short, a typical contract cleaning policy covers public liability (injury or damage you cause to third parties, including client property), employers' liability (claims from your employees, legally compulsory in almost all cases), and then optional sections you choose based on how you work: loss of keys, tools and equipment, damage to property worked upon or treatment risk, professional indemnity, employee dishonesty, and sometimes personal accident or business interruption. The exact wording, limits and exclusions vary between insurers, so the policy document always has the final say.

This guide walks through each section in turn, explains what it does and does not usually pay for, and gives you the questions to ask before you sign a schedule. If you want the summary of what we arrange for contract cleaning firms, the contract cleaners insurance page sets out the sections side by side.

Who needs contract cleaners insurance rather than a standard cleaning policy?

The label matters less than the work. Insurers use "contract cleaning" to describe a business that holds ongoing cleaning agreements with commercial clients: offices, schools, surgeries, gyms, industrial units, retail, common parts of blocks of flats. You usually have employees or regular subcontractors, you work unsupervised out of hours, you hold keys or access fobs, and your clients issue contracts with insurance clauses in them.

If you are a sole trader cleaning private homes with no staff, a domestic cleaners policy is usually the better fit. If most of your work is offices and shops but you have no formal long-term contracts, look at commercial and office cleaning insurance. Where contract cleaning differs is scale and accumulation of risk: more sites, more staff, more keys, higher limits demanded by clients, and more activities bolted on over time — window cleaning at height, periodic carpet work, washroom services, builders' cleans.

That accumulation is why a section-by-section review matters. Most gaps we see are not dramatic. They are a company that added external window cleaning at first-floor height two years ago and never told the insurer, or one that started holding a bunch of fifteen keys for a managing agent and assumed the liability section would pick it up.

Public liability: the core of contract cleaners insurance cover

Public liability responds when a third party — a client, a member of the public, a visitor, a tenant — suffers injury or property damage and you are legally responsible. It pays the compensation (called damages), plus the legal costs of defending or settling the claim, up to your limit of indemnity. The limit of indemnity is the most the insurer will pay for any one claim; the excess is the first slice of each claim you contribute yourself.

In contract cleaning, the realistic claims look like this:

  • An office worker slips on a corridor you have just mopped because the wet floor sign was left in the cupboard, fractures a wrist and is off work for months.
  • A cleaner catches a monitor with a vacuum hose and it falls off a desk.
  • A tap is left running in a third-floor washroom overnight and water comes through the ceiling into the suite below, damaging carpet, plasterboard and a client's stock.
  • A trailing cable across a reception trips a delivery driver.
  • Chemical is decanted into an unlabelled bottle and a client's member of staff is injured using it — which is where your COSHH arrangements get examined closely.

Limits are normally offered at £1m, £2m, £5m and £10m. Plenty of small commercial work is satisfied by £2m, but public sector, education, NHS, local authority and managing agent contracts frequently specify £5m or £10m. Our guide to public liability limits for cleaning contracts goes into how to read those clauses. As a rule, it is cheaper to buy the limit you will need for tenders than to increase it mid-year to win one job.

Watch two extensions in particular. First, damage to client property in your care, custody or control — some policies restrict cover for property you are working on or looking after, which is exactly the situation a cleaner is in all day. Second, indemnity to principal, which extends cover to the client or managing agent where a contract requires it. Both are commonly available and both are worth confirming in writing. For more on where liability actually attaches when you work inside someone else's building, see our guide on legal liability for cleaners entering client premises, or read the overview on the public liability insurance for cleaners page.

Employers' liability: the section you cannot choose to skip

If you employ anyone, the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 requires you to hold employers' liability insurance, and the standard minimum is £5 million. The HSE can fine a business up to £2,500 for each day it trades without valid cover, and you must make the certificate available to employees and to inspectors. Most insurers issue £10m as standard because that is what large contracts ask for.

This section covers claims from your own staff for injury or illness arising from their work: a cleaner who falls from a step ladder, a back injury from moving a scrubber dryer up a flight of stairs, dermatitis from repeated exposure to a degreaser, a hand caught in a machine, a needlestick injury during a washroom clean. Occupational disease claims can surface years after the employment ended, which is one reason you should keep old certificates and schedules indefinitely.

The question that catches contract cleaners out is labour-only subcontractors. If you engage self-employed cleaners but supply the materials and equipment and direct how the work is done, insurers generally treat them as if they were employees, and they need to be declared under the employers' liability section, not ignored. Genuine bona fide subcontractors — firms that quote for a job, carry their own insurance and work to their own methods — sit outside it, but you should still collect and diary their certificates. There is more detail on the employers' liability page and in our guide comparing public liability and employers' liability.

Damage to property worked upon and treatment risk

Here is the distinction that causes the most disappointment at claim stage. Public liability handles damage you cause incidentally — the vacuum that knocks over a vase. It often does not handle damage to the very thing you were paid to clean. If a carpet shrinks or the dye runs after a hot water extraction, if a limestone floor is etched by the wrong acidic product, if a stove enamel finish is stripped in a dip tank, if pressure washing forces water under a door threshold or blows the pointing out of a patio, that is a treatment risk or damage to property worked upon claim.

Some policies exclude it entirely. Some include a limited amount. Some offer it as a priced extension with its own limit and excess. If your contracts include periodic works — carpets, hard floors, stone, oven cleaning, façade or render cleaning — you should be asking for it explicitly. We have written a dedicated explanation in treatment risks: the gap in standard public liability, and it is a standard consideration on both carpet and upholstery cleaning cover and pressure washing cover.

Loss of keys, access fobs and alarm resets

Contract cleaners hold keys. Sometimes dozens, on one ring, for several clients. Lose that ring and the cost is not the key — it is replacing suites of locks and reprogramming access control across a building, plus the client's costs while security is compromised.

Loss of keys cover pays the cost of replacing locks and keys, and often the cost of recutting and reissuing, following loss or theft of client keys in your custody. Limits are typically modest (commonly in the low thousands per loss) so check the figure against a realistic worst case for your largest site. Sensible key discipline also keeps premiums and claims down: tagged with codes rather than addresses, signed in and out, never all on one ring, never left in a van. Our keyholding risks guide covers the operational side, and the loss of keys insurance page explains what the section pays for.

Tools, equipment, machines and stock

Liability sections cover harm to other people. They do nothing for your own property. A separate tools and equipment section covers your kit against theft, loss and accidental damage: scrubber dryers, rotaries, extraction machines, pressure washers, water-fed pole systems, industrial vacuums, ladders, cages and trolleys.

Points to check before you rely on it:

  • Overnight vehicle cover. Many policies exclude theft from an unattended vehicle overnight unless it is in a locked building or compound, or unless there was forced entry to a locked vehicle. Read the condition, not the summary.
  • Sum insured. Insure the cost to replace as new unless the policy says indemnity. Underinsurance can lead to a proportionate reduction in a claim payment.
  • Single article limit. Your £6,000 ride-on may exceed the maximum payable for any one item.
  • Hired-in plant. If you hire machines, you are usually liable under the hire agreement for damage and continuing hire charges. That needs specific cover.
  • Stock and consumables. Chemicals, paper goods and bin liners stored at your unit are business stock, not equipment.

Professional indemnity, money, dishonesty and other sections

Larger contract cleaners and facilities providers take on responsibilities beyond mopping. You write method statements, specify frequencies and products, advise on infection control, produce cleaning audits, hold TUPE-transferred staff, and occasionally manage subcontracted services. If a client alleges financial loss because your advice or specification was wrong — a validated deep clean that did not meet the standard promised, a specification that damaged a surface, a failure that closed a food site — that is a professional services allegation, and professional indemnity insurance is the section that responds. Note the retroactive date: professional indemnity works on a claims-made basis, meaning it covers claims notified during the policy year, but usually only for work carried out after that date. Keep the cover running continuously.

Other sections that appear in contract cleaning packages:

  • Employee dishonesty / fidelity guarantee. Theft of client cash or property by your own staff. Frequently excluded from liability cover, and a genuine exposure when cleaners work alone out of hours.
  • Personal accident. Benefits for the owner or staff following injury, useful when a working director cannot cover their rounds.
  • Business interruption and contents at your premises. If you run a unit or office with stock, machines and records.
  • Legal expenses. Employment tribunal defence, contract disputes and HSE prosecution defence costs, subject to conditions.
  • Cyber. You hold staff and client data, including site access details, and UK GDPR obligations apply. The ICO publishes practical guidance for small organisations.
  • Goods in transit and commercial vehicle cover. Motor is always a separate policy; equipment in the van may sit under either.

What is typically covered and what usually is not

ScenarioSection that usually respondsCommon catch
Visitor slips on a wet floor you moppedPublic liabilityExcess applies; signage evidence matters
Cleaner falls from a ladder at a client siteEmployers' liabilityMust be declared as employee or labour-only subcontractor
Vacuum knocks a client's laptop off a deskPublic liability (property damage)Care, custody and control restrictions
Carpet shrinks after extraction cleaningTreatment risk extensionExcluded on many standard policies
Client key ring lost, locks need replacingLoss of keysSection limit may be lower than the true cost
Scrubber dryer stolen from the van overnightTools and equipmentOvernight vehicle and forced-entry conditions
Cash taken from a client's office by a cleanerEmployee dishonestyNot covered by liability sections
Client claims a specification caused business lossProfessional indemnityClaims-made basis and retroactive date
Wear and tear, poor workmanship redone freeNoneInsurance is not a warranty for your own rework

Limits, excesses and the questions insurers will ask

Three numbers decide how useful a policy is in practice: the limit of indemnity per section, whether that limit is "any one claim" or "in the aggregate" for the year, and the excess. A £5m limit in the aggregate means £5m for all claims in the period combined. For most cleaning risks that is academic, but for a company with fifty sites it is worth knowing which you have.

As a commercial customer you also have a duty under the Insurance Act 2015 to make a fair presentation of risk — to disclose the material facts about your business clearly and accessibly, or at least give the insurer enough to ask sensible questions. Get it wrong and the insurer may be able to reduce or decline a claim. So expect to be asked:

  • Annual turnover, split by type of work, and your annual wageroll including labour-only subcontractors.
  • Number of employees, and how many are self-employed.
  • Types of premises you clean, and whether any are high risk (food production, laboratories, industrial, listed buildings, hospitals).
  • Maximum working height, and whether you use ladders, poles, towers, MEWPs or rope access.
  • Whether you hold client keys and how many.
  • Whether you undertake specialist work: builders' cleans, biohazard, needle sweeps, ductwork, kitchen extract, fogging. If you do, specialist and deep cleaning cover may be the right base policy.
  • Claims history, usually five years.
  • Whether you use any hot work, solvents or bulk chemical storage.

Answer these once and honestly and the quote you get will hold up. That is the thinking behind our questionnaire: it only asks the questions that apply to cleaning businesses, so you are not explaining your trade from scratch. If you already know what you need, you can start a contract cleaners insurance enquiry and we will come back with the sections priced separately so you can see what each one costs.

A practical checklist for reviewing your contract cleaning cover

  1. Pull out your current schedule, not the certificate, and list every section with its limit and excess.
  2. Check the public liability limit against the insurance clause in your three largest contracts. If a tender asks for £10m, note it now, not in the week of submission.
  3. Confirm the employers' liability limit is at least £5m and that every worker — including labour-only subcontractors — is inside the declared wageroll.
  4. Check whether damage to property worked upon or treatment risk is included, excluded or an extension, and at what limit.
  5. Count the client keys you actually hold and compare the total lock replacement cost to your loss of keys limit.
  6. Add up the replacement cost of your machines and check the sum insured and single article limit. Photograph serial numbers.
  7. Read the overnight vehicle theft condition word for word and change your parking habits if needed.
  8. List the services you have added since renewal: height, carpets, ovens, jet washing, builders' cleans, fogging. Tell your broker about all of them.
  9. Ask whether indemnity to principal and contractual liability wording can be confirmed, since managing agents often require it.
  10. Check you hold in-date certificates for every bona fide subcontractor, with a diary reminder for expiry.
  11. Make sure your method statements, COSHH assessments and signage practice match what you told the insurer. Claims defence depends on records more than memory — our note on the true cost of a cleaning claim explains why.
  12. Agree the internal process for reporting incidents within 24 hours, and share our steps for handling accidental damage with supervisors.

Putting the right package together

Contract cleaning insurance works best when it is assembled around how your company actually operates rather than bought as a fixed bundle. Two firms with the same turnover can need very different policies: one cleans twenty ground-floor offices with a small directly employed team, the other cleans three industrial sites at height with labour-only crews and £40,000 of machinery. Premiums reflect turnover, wageroll, work type, working height, claims history and the limits you choose, so any figure quoted without those details is guesswork.

If you want a second opinion on your current schedule, or you are pricing a tender that specifies limits you do not currently hold, send us the details through the contract cleaners insurance quote form and we will go through it section by section. You can also compare the full range of cleaning insurance covers or browse our other guides for cleaning businesses. This article is general guidance rather than personal advice — cover depends on the policy wording, insurer acceptance and your own circumstances, so talk it through with a broker before you rely on any one section.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is contract cleaners insurance one policy or several?

It is normally one policy containing several sections, each with its own limit, excess and conditions. Public liability and employers' liability are the core, with optional sections for loss of keys, tools and equipment, treatment risk, employee dishonesty and professional indemnity. Motor cover for your vans is always separate.

How much public liability do cleaning contracts usually require?

It varies by client. Many private commercial contracts accept £2m, while public sector, education, healthcare and managing agent contracts commonly specify £5m or £10m. Read the insurance clause before you tender, because raising a limit mid-contract is possible but less convenient than buying the right level at renewal.

Does my policy cover the cleaners I take on as self-employed?

It depends on how they work. If you supply the materials and equipment and direct the work, insurers generally treat them as labour-only subcontractors and they must be declared and rated under employers' liability. Genuine bona fide subcontractors who carry their own insurance sit outside it, but you should still collect and check their certificates.

Am I covered if we damage the floor we were cleaning?

Not always under standard public liability. Damage to the item you were paid to work on is often excluded or restricted, and is usually addressed by a damage to property worked upon or treatment risk extension. If your contracts include carpets, stone, hard floors, ovens or pressure washing, ask for that extension specifically.

What happens if I forget to tell the insurer we started working at height?

Working height is a material fact. Under the Insurance Act 2015 duty of fair presentation, failing to disclose it could allow the insurer to reduce, decline or avoid a claim, or to apply different terms. Tell your broker as soon as a new service or a new type of site starts, even mid-year — mid-term adjustments are routine.

Does contract cleaners insurance cover theft by one of my cleaners?

Liability sections generally exclude dishonest acts by your own employees. Cover for client cash or property stolen by staff usually sits under an employee dishonesty or fidelity guarantee section, which has its own limit and conditions, often including reference checks and a requirement to report to the police.

title: Window Cleaners Insurance and Working at Height Explained
excerpt: Height is the single biggest factor in how insurers price and accept window cleaning risks. Here is how ladders, water-fed poles, cradles and rope access are treated, and what you need to have in place.
metaTitle: Window Cleaners Insurance & Working at Height
metaDescription: How working at height affects window cleaners insurance: ladders, water-fed poles, height limits, what insurers ask and the safety records that support cover.
keywords: window cleaners insurance working at height
working at height regulations window cleaning
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Window cleaner using a water-fed pole from ground level to clean upper-floor windows on a house
content:
If you clean windows for a living, height is the one thing an insurer will always want to talk about. Not your round size, not your cleaning solution, not how long you have been trading — how high you go, and how you get there. Most window cleaning policies are written with a working height limit, a maximum height above ground level at which you are covered to work. Go above it and a claim arising from that job may not be paid, even though the rest of your policy is perfectly valid.

The short answer for most rounds: if you work from the ground with a water-fed pole and only use ladders occasionally for low-level domestic work, you sit in the part of the market insurers are most comfortable with. If you use ladders as your main method, work above two or three storeys, or use cradles, mobile elevating work platforms or rope access, the questions get more detailed, the wording matters more and fewer insurers will take the risk. None of that means you cannot get cover — it means the way you describe your work needs to be accurate.

This guide explains how height is treated in window cleaners insurance, what the Work at Height Regulations actually require (ladders are not banned), the questions underwriters ask, and the practical records that support both your premium and any claim you have to make. It is general guidance rather than advice about your own policy — cover always depends on the wording, the insurer and your circumstances.

How does working at height affect window cleaners insurance?

Height affects three things: whether an insurer will quote at all, the price, and the conditions attached to the policy.

The reason is simple. A fall from height is one of the most common causes of serious workplace injury in Great Britain, and the consequences are expensive. An injured self-employed window cleaner loses income and may never return to ladder work. An injured employee can bring a claim against your business that runs into six figures once care costs and loss of earnings are added. A dropped pole section or bucket from the second floor can cause a head injury to a passer-by. Height turns a modest job into a potentially catastrophic claim, so underwriters price it carefully.

Most window cleaning policies handle this with a height condition. It usually appears in one of three forms:

  • A stated maximum working height in metres — for example cover applies to work carried out up to a specified height above ground level, with anything higher excluded unless agreed.
  • A storey limit — cover for ground floor and first floor only, or up to three storeys, again with higher work needing specific agreement.
  • A method condition — cover for reach-and-wash pole work from ground level, with ladder work limited or excluded, or ladder use permitted only up to a certain height.

Read your schedule and endorsements before you take on a taller building. If your policy is capped at, say, third-floor level and a managing agent asks you to add a five-storey block, that is a phone call to your broker, not a decision to make on site.

What do the Work at Height Regulations 2005 require?

The Work at Height Regulations 2005 apply to employers, the self-employed and anyone who controls work at height. They are risk-based rather than prescriptive, and there is one myth worth killing straight away: ladders are not banned. The Health and Safety Executive has said so repeatedly. A ladder is a legitimate piece of access equipment for low-risk, short-duration work where a more substantial platform is not justified.

What the regulations do require is a sensible order of thinking:

  1. Avoid work at height where you reasonably can. For window cleaning, this is exactly what a water-fed pole does — it brings the work to ground level.
  2. Where you cannot avoid it, use equipment or other measures to prevent a fall. A tower, a MEWP with guard rails, a properly maintained cradle.
  3. Where the risk cannot be eliminated, minimise the distance and consequences of a fall. Harness and fall-arrest systems, correct anchor points.

You also need to plan the work, take account of weather, make sure the people doing it are competent, and inspect equipment. For sole traders that does not mean a filing cabinet of paperwork — it means a written risk assessment for the types of work you do, a short site-specific check when something is unusual, and ladder inspection records you can actually produce.

Where equipment such as a suspended cradle or a MEWP is used, the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 (LOLER) bring in thorough examination requirements, which is why insurers ask for inspection certificates when cradles appear on a proposal form.

Ladders versus water-fed poles: how insurers see the difference

Reach-and-wash systems changed the risk profile of the trade. Working from the ground removes the fall, and that is reflected in how readily insurers quote. But poles bring their own hazards, and it is a mistake to assume a pole round is a zero-risk round.

FactorLadder workWater-fed pole work
Main injury riskFall from height to the cleaner; ladder slipping or being knockedManual handling and strain; trips over hoses; falling pole sections
Third-party injury riskDropped tools or buckets; ladder falling onto a person or vehiclePassers-by slipping on wet paving; pole contact with a person
Property damage riskLadder feet on conservatory roofs, gutters, flowerbeds, car bonnetsWater through open windows or trickle vents; damaged seals and rotten frames; brush marks on soft stonework
Electrical riskContact with overhead lines or service cablesCarbon fibre poles conduct — contact with overhead lines can be fatal
Typical insurer attitudeAccepted, with height conditions and questions about training and footingGenerally the preferred method; broader appetite and easier acceptance

Two points catch people out. First, carbon fibre poles conduct electricity. Working near overhead lines, service cables into a property, or street lighting columns with damaged covers is a genuine hazard, and insurers will expect you to have thought about it. Second, water damage is the most common pole-related property claim we see discussed in the trade: a flat or trickle vent left open, water tracking behind a failed seal, and a ceiling stain in the room below. That is a damage to property claim under your public liability section — and if the damage is to the very thing you were cleaning rather than the surrounding property, you may be into damage to property worked upon territory, which is not always included as standard. Our guide to treatment risks and the gap in standard public liability explains that distinction in more detail.

What questions will an insurer ask about height?

Underwriting a window cleaning risk is mostly about access method. Expect some version of the following, and expect to answer accurately, because the duty of fair presentation under the Insurance Act 2015 requires commercial customers to disclose every material circumstance they know or ought to know. Getting this wrong is how a claim gets reduced or declined.

  • What is your maximum working height? Give the real figure, including the occasional job, not the everyday average.
  • What proportion of work is ground-level pole, ladder, tower, MEWP or cradle? A rough percentage split is fine.
  • Do you use ladders, and to what height? Say whether they are used for access, for working from, or only for gutter clearance.
  • Do you ever use rope access or abseiling? This is usually excluded from standard cleaning policies and needs a specialist market and IRATA-qualified operatives.
  • Do you work on cradles or building maintenance units, and are LOLER examination certificates in place?
  • What training have you and your staff had? Ladder Association, PASMA for mobile towers, IPAF for MEWPs.
  • Do you clean internal atrium or stairwell glazing? Different access, different fall consequences.
  • Do you also offer gutter vacuuming, solar panel cleaning, pressure washing or roof work? Anything beyond glass needs declaring so the description of business is correct.
  • Do you use subcontractors, and are they labour-only or bona fide? Labour-only subcontractors work under your direction and are usually treated as employees for insurance purposes; bona fide subcontractors carry their own policies and you should collect evidence.
  • Claims and incidents in the last five years, including near misses you reported to a client.

When you get a quote through our window cleaners insurance enquiry form, these are the questions you will see — and not much else. There is no point asking a sole-trader window cleaner about stock in transit or catering equipment.

Which covers matter most when you work at height?

Height does not create a separate policy section. It changes the severity of claims under sections you already need.

CoverWhat it does for height work
Public liabilityInjury to a member of the public or damage to third-party property — a dropped tool, a ladder into a parked car, water through an open window. Most window cleaning contracts specify a limit of indemnity (the maximum payable for a claim) of £1m, £2m or £5m.
Employers' liabilityLegally required if you have employees, including most labour-only subcontractors. Fall-from-height injury claims are among the most expensive an employer faces.
Tools and equipmentPoles, brush heads, purified water systems, filter vessels, reels and reach-and-wash tanks. Van-stored equipment usually has overnight security conditions.
Personal accidentBenefits for you if a fall stops you working. Liability cover pays other people; it does nothing for your own lost income.
Loss of keysRelevant if you hold fobs or gate keys for commercial sites and communal blocks.

On limits: the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 requires a minimum of £5 million of employers' liability cover, and most policies in the market are issued at £10 million. The HSE can fine a business up to £2,500 for each day it trades without valid cover. If you have even one part-time employee or a regular labour-only helper, read our explainer on employers' liability for cleaning companies before you assume you are exempt.

For public liability, let the contract decide rather than guessing. Local authorities, housing associations and managing agents frequently specify £5 million for work on their buildings, and some facilities management tenders go to £10 million. Our guide to choosing a public liability limit for cleaning contracts covers how to match your limit to what you are being asked to sign. If you need broader detail on the individual sections, the public liability page and the tools and equipment page set out the typical structure.

Real claim scenarios from height work

Illustrative examples, not real claims, but each one reflects a pattern that comes up in this trade.

  • The knocked ladder. A cleaner sets a ladder against a shopfront in a narrow high street. A delivery driver reverses, clips the base, and the ladder goes into the shop window. Third-party glass, shop closure, and an injury to the cleaner. Public liability responds to the glass; employers' liability or personal accident deals with the person, depending on employment status.
  • Water through a trickle vent. Pole work on a first-floor flat, vent open, water runs down inside the reveal and stains the plaster and a rug. Modest sum, but the client wants a decorator, not a promise. Our guide on handling accidental damage sets out what to do in the first hour.
  • Conservatory roof. Ladder foot placed on a polycarbonate panel to reach a bedroom window. The panel gives way, the cleaner falls partway through, and the whole roof section needs replacing.
  • Dropped pole section. A worn clamp lets a pole section slide and fall three storeys onto a pavement, catching a pedestrian's shoulder. Injury claims like this turn on inspection and maintenance records.
  • Slip on wet paving. Purified water runs across a supermarket entrance, a customer slips, and the store's insurers pursue you. The obvious defence is signage and hose management, which is why insurers ask about it.

The financial hit is rarely just the repair. Excess, lost days, a client relationship and possibly your renewal terms all move. We set out the full picture in the true cost of a cleaning claim.

A practical working-at-height checklist for window cleaners

Work through this before your next renewal or your next tender.

  1. Write down your real maximum working height and check it against your policy schedule. If the schedule is lower than your round, call your broker.
  2. Keep a written risk assessment covering ladder use, pole use, overhead cables, wet surfaces and public areas. One or two pages, dated and reviewed annually.
  3. Do a site-specific check on anything unusual — awkward ground, fragile roofs, overhead lines, school or hospital access rules.
  4. Inspect ladders before use and record formal inspections. Look at stiles, feet, rungs and locking mechanisms. Retire damaged ladders rather than repairing them.
  5. Use ladder stabilisers, standoffs or footing devices where appropriate, and never rest a ladder on gutters, conservatories or glazing bars.
  6. Check pole clamps and sections weekly and keep a maintenance note. Replace worn collars before they slip.
  7. Treat every overhead line as live. Plan the route and angle of carbon poles away from cables, and do not carry poles upright near lines.
  8. Manage water and hoses in public areas: cones or wet floor signs, hoses routed against the building, and a check that ground-floor windows and vents are closed.
  9. Get training and keep the certificates — Ladder Association, PASMA, IPAF as relevant. Tenders ask for them and insurers like to see them.
  10. Collect evidence of insurance from bona fide subcontractors and record which of your people are labour-only.
  11. Set a weather rule and stick to it. Wind is the main one for pole work; a written threshold protects you when a client pushes.
  12. Record near misses. A short log of what nearly happened shows an underwriter a business that manages risk rather than hopes.

When your round includes more than glass

Plenty of window cleaners add gutter clearance, fascia and soffit cleaning, solar panel washing, conservatory roofs and driveway work. Each addition changes your risk and needs to appear in your description of business. Gutter vacuuming from the ground is usually straightforward; gutter clearance from a ladder is not the same job as cleaning a pane of glass, and roof access is a different conversation entirely.

If jet washing has become a regular earner, look at how pressure washing and driveway cleaning cover is arranged, because high-pressure work brings its own damage exposures — pointing blown out of brickwork, flooded airbricks, overspray on neighbouring cars. If you have moved into office and communal-area work, commercial cleaning insurance may be the better fit, and if you hold fobs for blocks of flats then loss of keys cover is worth a look. You can see the full range on the cleaning insurance hub or browse the rest of our guides.

Getting your height cover right

The businesses that get the smoothest renewals are the ones who can describe their access methods precisely, produce a risk assessment and a ladder inspection record, and show training certificates. That is not bureaucracy for its own sake — it is the evidence an underwriter uses to decide whether you are a careful operator or an unknown quantity, and it is the evidence that supports you if a claim is ever disputed.

If you are not sure whether your current policy covers the heights you actually work at, or a new contract has asked for a limit you do not hold, tell us what your round looks like and we will work through the wording with you. Start with our window cleaners insurance quote form, which only asks the questions that apply to window cleaning, or use the general enquiry page if your business covers several types of cleaning. Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a height limit on window cleaners insurance?

Most policies carry some form of working height condition, expressed either in metres above ground level, in storeys, or as a restriction on access method. There is no single industry figure — it varies by insurer and by how you work. Check your schedule and any endorsements, and speak to your broker before taking on a building taller than your stated limit.

Are ladders banned for window cleaning in the UK?

No. The Health and Safety Executive is clear that ladders are not banned. Under the Work at Height Regulations 2005 you must avoid work at height where reasonably practicable, and where you cannot, choose suitable equipment. A ladder can be the right choice for short-duration, low-risk work, provided it is in good condition, correctly footed and used by someone competent.

Is water-fed pole work cheaper to insure than ladder work?

Ground-level pole work generally attracts a broader insurer appetite because it removes the fall risk, and that often shows in the terms offered. It is not automatic, and premium depends on your turnover, claims history, heights worked, employees and the other services you offer. Pole work still carries water damage, slip and overhead cable risks that insurers take into account.

Do I need employers' liability insurance if I use a labour-only helper?

Usually yes. Labour-only subcontractors work under your direction and using your equipment, so they are typically treated as employees for insurance purposes. The Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 requires a minimum of £5 million cover, and the HSE can fine a business up to £2,500 for each day it operates without it. If you are unsure how your helper is classified, ask your broker before the next job.

Does public liability cover me if I fall off a ladder?

No. Public liability covers injury to third parties and damage to their property. Your own injury is not covered by it. If you are self-employed, personal accident cover is the section that provides benefits when an injury stops you working. If the injured person is your employee, employers' liability is the relevant cover.

What records should I keep to support a height-related claim?

Keep your written risk assessments, ladder and equipment inspection records, training certificates, a near-miss log, before-and-after photographs of jobs where damage is a possibility, and any correspondence with the client about access arrangements. Dated evidence that you planned the work and maintained your equipment is what supports both your defence and your insurer's handling of the claim.
